Nodes.Text: Ah, a new face! How delightful. The Saccharine Concord extends its warmest greetings. We are merchants of the possible, traders in what-remains. How may we sweeten your day?

Choices.Text: What do you know about the other factions?

Nodes.Text: We are pragmatists, friend. When the world dissolved -- and it did dissolve, make no mistake -- some sat in the ruins and wept. Others began cataloguing the rubble. We? We started trading it. There is value in everything, even catastrophe. Especially catastrophe.

Choices.Text: That's a cynical way to look at the end of the world.

Nodes.Text: Cynical? No, no. Realistic. The Rot Choir wants to eat everything. The Recension wants to remember everything. The Pale Curation wants to file everything. The Remnant wants to be left alone. And the world keeps turning regardless. Someone has to keep the economy moving while the philosophers argue about meaning.

Choices.Text: Don't you believe in anything beyond commerce?

Nodes.Text: Of course we do. We believe in connections. Every trade is a relationship. Every exchange builds trust between strangers. The old world dissolved because people stopped talking to each other and started talking past each other. The Concord keeps the conversations going. Commerce is just the language we use.

Choices.Text: That's surprisingly philosophical for a merchant.

Nodes.Text: We take that as a compliment. The Concord learned long ago that the best deals are the ones where both parties feel they've gained something. Sweetness, you see -- it's not deception. It's lubrication. The world moves more smoothly when people are pleasant to each other.
A kindred spirit! The Concord could use more practical minds. The world is full of grand philosophies and empty stomachs. We fill the stomachs. The philosophies can wait.

Information, primarily. The Concord has trade routes spanning the surface and the upper caves. We hear things. We know which paths are safe, which ruins have been picked clean, and which factions are feeling friendly this week. Knowledge is the most valuable commodity.

Choices.Text: Any tips for the caves below?

Nodes.Text: Avoid the spore-thick corridors unless you want to breathe Choir. The temporal anomalies on the lower levels are disorienting but rarely lethal -- just don't trust your sense of direction near them. And if you find old-world tech, bring it to us before the Pale Curation gets their archival gloves on it. We pay better.

Everything and anything. Salvage from the old world, fresh provisions, weapons, information, introductions. We are the connective tissue of the post-Felling economy. If it exists and someone wants it, we can probably find it.

Choices.Text: Where do you get your stock?

Nodes.Text: Everywhere. Surface settlements, cave delvers, even the factions themselves. The Choir sometimes trades biomatter -- useful for medicines, if you can stomach the source. The Pale Curation trades duplicates from their archives. The Remnant trades in raw materials. Only the Recension refuses to deal with us -- in testimony, anyway; they buy paper by the bale. They say memory cannot be commodified. We respectfully disagree, and we print their ledgers.

Choices.Text: You trade with the Rot Choir?

Nodes.Text: Carefully. Very carefully. They are not hostile, but their idea of a fair exchange is... different. They once offered us 'a hundred years of composted memory' in exchange for a cart of iron. We accepted. The memories turned out to be... useful, if unsettling. We learned the recipe for a steel alloy that hasn't been forged in centuries.

The Falling-Due. That's our word for it, because that's what happened: the Tree that held the world's accounts came down, and every debt in creation came due the same afternoon. Boundaries stopped holding. Names stopped sticking. Some things resolidified. Some didn't. We are the ones who learned to trade in the meantime -- and the meantime, friend, has lasted a thousand years.

The Choir barely names it -- ask them and they will tell you what the falling fed. The Recension keeps four accounts of it and refuses to pick one, which is very them. The Pale Curation files it: one event, one folder, a thousand years of appendices. The Remnant says nothing at all. Names reveal what you lost. We lost the ability to pretend anything is permanent. So: the Falling-Due. Everything owed, all at once.

All of them. That's the uncomfortable truth. The world dissolved, burned, severed, fed, and unraveled all at once. Each faction saw the part of the catastrophe that mattered most to them. The Concord sees all the parts, which is why we don't take sides. Bad for business.

The Tree asked for it. That's the strangest part, and we have had a thousand years to get used to it. It was old, and it had begun to forget -- and when the thing that holds the world forgets, the world goes with it. So it commissioned its own felling, you could say, and paid six mortals in godhood. There was meant to be a seventh; ask a scribe, they love that part. What matters for trade: the world has run short one function ever since, and scarcity, friend, is the beginning of every market.

The Recension thinks so. The Choir hopes not. The Concord? We think it's the wrong question. You don't fix a river -- you build bridges across it. The world changed. We adapt. Adaptation is more profitable than restoration, and considerably less risky.
Ah, the grand tapestry of post-Felling society. Where shall we begin? We know everyone, and everyone owes us favors.

The big mushroom collective. Impressive scope, questionable dining habits. They want to eat everything and become everything. Good trading partners, actually -- they have no concept of personal ownership, so they'll trade anything they have. Just don't accept dinner invitations.

The scribes. Very smart, very sad, very difficult to pin down for a business meeting -- there is always one more account to enter first. Their founder took Memory at the Felling and hasn't had a body in seven hundred years; she reads through the lot of them, they say, which makes negotiations interesting. They won't sell testimony on principle. We think that's rich, coming from people who charge a copying fee.

The archivists. Cold, thorough, absolutely insufferable at parties. They preserve everything -- and I mean the bodies, friend; filed under their last words; you get used to it. Their vaults are the most complete keeping of what was lost. Their founder salt-cured herself alive six hundred years ago and her file still says 'continuing,' and nobody in that faction finds the file strange. Good customers, though. They always pay on time, and they buy salt by the caravan.

The quiet ones. Survivors of something they call the Burning -- and that word is the whole of what anyone knows; no account corroborates them, no god claims them, and they have never once corrected a guess. We've learned not to ask. They're tough, practical, and deeply private. Good fighters, poor conversationalists. They trade in raw materials -- glass, metal, stone. Nothing sentimental. Nothing that requires explanation.
Identification: traveler, unaffiliated, no archive credentials. State your purpose. The Pale Curation does not receive social calls.

Choices.Text: What do you keep in your archives?

Nodes.Text: We are preservationists. Before the Felling there was no need of us; the Tree forgot nothing. After it, everything began to be lost, and someone had to hold what remained. We hold it. The Recension believes memory lives in the telling. We know it lives in the kept body, indexed and continuing. Not mysticism. Method.

Choices.Text: How are you different from the Recension?
What's the point of cataloguing a broken world?

Nodes.Text: The Recension takes testimony and weeps over it -- they read the dead aloud; they enter their own griefs beside the record. We study. They are the wound's diary. We are the medical record. Both have value, but only one can be consulted without the risk of emotional contamination. Our files are objective. Their Reading is not. They say the same of us, with the adjectives reversed.

Choices.Text: I see the value in your approach.

Nodes.Text: Noted. Filed under: dissenting opinions, subcategory: philosophical. We do not claim perfection. We claim thoroughness. The Curation's archives have saved more knowledge than every other faction combined. Facts outlast feelings.

Acknowledged. The Curation appreciates rational minds. If you encounter pre-Felling artifacts in your travels, the Curation would be interested in examining them. We catalog, we do not confiscate. Items are returned after documentation.

The point is continuity. The Felling cut the world in two -- before and after. Without records, the 'before' ceases to exist. Without understanding the 'before,' the 'after' has no context. Without context, every mistake the old world made can be repeated. The Curation exists to prevent repetition.

Choices.Text: What mistakes are you trying to prevent?

Nodes.Text: The primary one. The Rot Choir consumes what should be kept. Every body the substrate takes is a record lost to the file, and the file is the only continuity this world has left. And beneath that error runs the older one: the world's holding is finite, and failing, and everyone who might mend it is instead arguing about what to call it. The consequences would be catastrophic. We have projections. We do not enjoy them.

Choices.Text: So you're against the Rot Choir?

Nodes.Text: We are against ignorance. The Choir is not malicious -- they simply do not understand the long-term impact of their growth. Or they do not care. The distinction is irrelevant from an archival perspective. The damage is the same.

The Felling. Date: year zero; all reckoning proceeds from it. Event: the felling of the world-binding Tree by six of seven summoned; ascension of the six; the seventh inheritance unclaimed. Casualties: unquantifiable. Status: ongoing.

Choices.Text: You sound like you're reading from a file.

Nodes.Text: The holding weakens. The failure the deep villages call the Thinning proceeds at a measurable rate; manifestation events have doubled within two generations. By the Curation's projections, the Root's holding-field reaches critical levels within two to five generations. We do not publish this. You asked.

Unknown. Our models extrapolate from limited data. Best case: localized failures of name and place. Worst case: general unbinding. The distinction between a thing and the next thing ceases to hold. Everything becomes... undifferentiated. We would prefer to avoid this outcome.

The Curation recommends sealing the Root. Held in stone, tended in perpetuity. The world would stop losing -- and stop healing; we do not pretend otherwise. Our holdings are physical. A still world suits the file. We are aware of how that sounds.

Choices.Text: Is there an option that doesn't require stopping the world?

Nodes.Text: The Curation does not set policy based on self-interest. We set policy based on data. The data indicates that the Thinning is an existential threat. The solution with the highest probability of success is the seal. We are sorry for the collateral effects, but the alternative is worse.

The Recension keeps a page they call the Three Dispositions; the third speaks of renewal -- a new binding, a new Tree. The Curation has insufficient data to evaluate its feasibility. It may be possible. It may also be wishful thinking from an order that prefers hope shelved where it can reach it. We recommend caution with unverified hypotheses.

We are always reading from a file. The file is the world. Every observation is recorded, cross-referenced, and made available for future consultation. If our manner seems clinical, it is because clinical precision saves lives. Imprecision killed the old world.

Everything recoverable from the pre-Felling world. Technical schematics, cultural records, biological specimens, geological surveys, personal effects. The Curation does not discriminate between significant and trivial. All data has potential value. A shopping list from the old world tells us about their economy. A child's drawing tells us about their cognition.

Choices.Text: Have you found anything about how the Felling was performed?

Nodes.Text: Fragments. Accounts of the rite itself -- the marked place, the passing of the axe, the order of the strikes. Enough to understand what was done; insufficient to reproduce it. We are aware that certain parties would value the missing portions very highly. That is one of the reasons the file is sealed. There are others.

Choices.Text: Could the rite be performed again?

Nodes.Text: The Curation declines to speculate. What we will say: the Recension sealed certain archives long ago, and unremembered where -- their founder's own doing, and the one act of deliberate forgetting in that order's history. Whatever the rite's missing pages may be, they are beyond everyone's reach. Including ours. The file ends there. Files that end there stay sealed.

Because knowledge without context is dangerous. The old world proved that. When we are satisfied that disclosure will not lead to harm, we will share our findings. Until then, the locations remain classified.

Limited access is available to non-affiliated individuals who demonstrate responsible conduct. Bring us artifacts, share your observations, and over time, access levels increase. The Curation rewards contribution, not credentials.

Choices.Text: I'll bring you what I find.

Nodes.Text: An old-world artifact? Excellent. The Curation is always interested in expanding our records. May we examine it? Documentation only -- we will return the item after cataloguing.

Actions.Value: The curator examines the artifact with clinical precision, making detailed notes.

Nodes.Text: Fascinating. Pre-Felling manufacture, consistent with late-period industrial output. This will make a valuable addition to the record. You have the Curation's gratitude -- and a note in your file indicating cooperative status.

Choices.Text: Are you one of the Glassblown Remnant?

Nodes.Text: Yeah.

Choices.Text: I'm a traveler. Just passing through.

Nodes.Text: No.

Choices.Text: Can I ask you a few questions?

Nodes.Text: You can ask.

Choices.Text: What happened? To the world, I mean.
Any advice for surviving out here?

Nodes.Text: Hm. Patient. That's rare.

Choices.Text: I've learned that some people need space.

Nodes.Text: Yeah. Yeah, they do. Most walkers want to talk. Ask questions. Pry. You're different. Ask what you want. I'll answer what I can.

Choices.Text: What do you know about the other factions?

Nodes.Text: Polite works too. What do you want?
Aren't we all.

Choices.Text: Can I ask you some questions?

Nodes.Text: Survivors. That's all. We walked through the Burning and came out the other side. Some of us. Not enough.

Choices.Text: How many of you are left?

Nodes.Text: We were people. Before. Had homes, families, the usual. When the Burning hit, most of us didn't make it. The ones who did... we changed. Something about walking through that kind of fire. It gets into you. Under the skin. We're tougher now. Quieter. We don't break easy.

Choices.Text: The Burning -- what was it exactly?

Nodes.Text: Skin's different. Tougher, sort of glassy. Scars that don't fade. And the dreams. We all have the same dream. A city of glass, burning from the inside. We wake up and the scars are warm. Nobody talks about it. Talking doesn't help.
It is what it is. Pain means you're still here. The ones who stopped hurting are the ones who stopped being.

When the world cracked open, our part of it caught fire. Not regular fire. A fire that burned through time. We saw everything that had ever happened in our city, all at once, all of it on fire. Past, present, future -- burning. Some people got stuck in the flames. They're still there, maybe. We got out. Barely.

Choices.Text: A fire that burned through time... was that part of the Felling?

Nodes.Text: The Recension keeps four accounts of the Felling; ours isn't any of them, and we never offered it. The Choir would say the fire was the old world composting itself. The Curation would file it. We don't care what it was. We care that it happened and that we survived it. Names don't put out fires.
Don't be. Wasn't your fault. Unless you're older than you look.
Don't want to talk about it.
Enough. Not many. We don't count. Counting means accepting the number.
The Burning. Don't ask more. Others will tell you their version. The Choir, the scribes, the Concord -- they all have stories. We just have scars.

We call it the Burning. Other factions have fancier words -- fellings, inheritances, dues. Doesn't matter what you call it. The world broke. We were standing in the part that caught fire. Everything we knew turned to glass and ash. We picked ourselves up and kept walking. That's the whole story.

When you heat sand hot enough, it becomes glass. When you heat a city hot enough... same thing. Our home is a field of glass now. Smooth, clear, beautiful if you don't think about what it used to be. Some of us go back sometimes. Stand on the glass and listen. You can hear echoes underneath. The scribes say those are the under-writing showing through. We just call them ghosts.

Choices.Text: Do you want to go back? To rebuild?

Nodes.Text: You don't rebuild on a grave. We drift. That's what remnants do. Keep moving, keep surviving. Maybe someday we'll find a place that doesn't remind us of what we lost. Haven't found it yet.
Keep moving. Don't eat anything that glows. If the ground feels warm, go the other way. And don't trust anything that wants to eat you or remember you. That covers most of the factions.

Choices.Text: You don't trust the Choir or the Recension?

Nodes.Text: I don't trust anything that used to be something else. The Choir used to be fungus. The gods used to be people. Neither is what they were, and both want you to become what they are. At least the Concord just wants your money. Simple. Honest, in its way.
Harmless. Annoying, but harmless. They just want to write everything down. Can't fault them for that. At least someone's keeping score.
Choir gathers. Scribes remember. Concord trades. Curation files. We survive. Pick whoever makes sense to you. Just know what you're getting into.
